T2 Mac fan control guide

t2fanrd on Omarchy

Fan control for T2 Macs — one package, one config file, no more jet-engine fans.

Reviewed 2026-11-17 · independent editorial guide

Short answer

Install t2fanrd with omarchy pkg add t2fanrd and start it with sudo systemctl enable --now t2fanrd. It drives the fans from your CPU temperature on a curve in /etc/t2fand.conf. Note: upstream was archived Nov 16, 2026 — the hwmon + fancontrol route is the maintained future.

On this page Install Getting started Common issues Comparison Switch from macOS fan control Questions

t2fanrd on Omarchy

t2fanrd is a free, open-source fan control daemon for Intel Macs with the Apple T2 chip — it reads your CPU temperature and drives the fans on a curve you configure, so a T2 Mac running Omarchy stays cool without sounding like a jet engine.

TL;DR

omarchy pkg add t2fanrd
sudo systemctl enable --now t2fanrd

It takes ~2 minutes (263 KB download, 530.4 KB installed). Then enable and start the service. That's the install. There is no window to open — t2fanrd is a background daemon. It creates its config automatically on first run.

Read this before you install: the upstream project was archived on Nov 16, 2026 — the same day this package landed in the Omarchy store. The maintainer's reason: recent kernels expose the fans through the standard hwmon interface, so "standard userspace fan daemons should work" once you write 1 to /sys/module/macsmc_hwmon/parameters/fan_control. The Omarchy package (version r16.48baf96-2) is built from the sharpenedblade fork, which the archived README points to for anyone who wants to keep the t2fand config format. t2fanrd is still the simplest path — one package, one config file, no hwmon wrangling — but it is effectively unmaintained upstream, and the hwmon + fancontrol route is the future the maintainer points to. Both paths are covered below.

Getting started (5 minutes)

1. Install and start the daemon.

Run the two commands above. The service is t2fanrd.service; check it actually started:

systemctl status t2fanrd

If it says active (running), the daemon is in control of your fans. If it failed, read the log before anything else — the two most common failures are covered in "Common issues" below:

journalctl -xeu t2fanrd

2. See your fans and temperatures.

t2fanrd itself prints nothing to your screen — watch it through sensors (from lm_sensors):

sensors

Look for two blocks: coretemp-isa-0000 (CPU package temperature — this is the number the fan curve reads) and applesmc-acpi-0 (fan RPM, min/max). A healthy idle looks roughly like CPU ~40–50 °C with fans near their minimum (~1200–2000 RPM depending on model). Under load the RPM should climb as the temperature passes your low_temp.

3. Tune the curve.

Config lives in /etc/t2fand.conf (note the name — t2fand, not t2fanrd — a leftover from the original Python daemon this was rewritten from). It's created automatically on first run, one section per fan:

[Fan1]
low_temp=55
high_temp=75
speed_curve=linear
always_full_speed=false
  • low_temp — the temperature where the fan starts speeding up (default 55 °C).
  • high_temp — the temperature where the fan hits maximum speed (default 75 °C).
  • speed_curve — linear, exponential, or logarithmic. Linear ramps evenly; exponential stays quiet longer then climbs fast; logarithmic climbs early then flattens. The README includes a curve graph if you want to see them.
  • always_full_speed — set true and that fan runs at max no matter what. A panic button, not a daily setting.

After editing, restart the daemon — it reads the config at startup:

sudo systemctl restart t2fanrd

The 3 things you need to know:

  • It only watches the CPU. The daemon reads one temperature — the CPU package sensor (coretemp temp1_input) — and drives every fan from it. If your GPU is the hot part (gaming, rendering on a dual-GPU MacBook Pro or a Mac Pro), the fans may not respond. See issue #3 below.
  • It takes manual control of the fans from the SMC. The daemon writes 1 to each fan's fan*_manual sysfs file and then sets speed through fan*_output. The firmware's own fan curve stops applying while the daemon runs — which is the point, and also why the suspend bug below matters.
  • There is no GUI and no status command. Everything is systemctl status t2fanrd, journalctl -xeu t2fanrd, sensors, and /etc/t2fand.conf. If you want a window with dials, this is not that tool.

Config location.

/etc/t2fand.conf — created automatically on first run. There is no app to open and no per-user config.

Practical notes: On Omarchy, omarchy-update upgrades t2fanrd with the rest of the system; restart the service afterwards (sudo systemctl restart t2fanrd) so the new binary is the one running. To remove it: sudo systemctl disable --now t2fanrd, then omarchy pkg drop t2fanrd. Your config in /etc/t2fand.conf is left behind — delete it by hand if you want a clean slate.

Common issues & fixes

All of these come from the project's own GitHub issues — they are real reports from T2 Mac owners, including one filed from Omarchy itself, not guesses. Each one is still marked for on-machine confirmation in the checklist above.

"Error: Cannot write to fan controller" — service fails to start

sudo systemctl enable --now t2fanrd fails, and running sudo t2fanrd by hand ends with Error: Cannot write to fan controller (sometimes surfacing as an "Input/Output error"). The daemon found your fans but can't write to them.

Fix: This is a kernel/driver problem, not a t2fanrd bug — the maintainer's own diagnosis, and a later contributor confirmed it as a kernel bug in the T2 patches that t2fanrd cannot work around. First, make sure you are actually running a T2-patched kernel (see the linux-t2 sibling app — a stock Arch kernel has no T2 fan driver at all). If you are on the T2 kernel and still hit it, the issue thread points to the t2linux patches repo — there is no known fix inside t2fanrd, and the older Python t2fand hits the same error. Report it upstream with your model identifier (MacBookPro16,1, etc.) and kernel version.

Fans stop responding after suspend — daemon looks fine but isn't

After waking from suspend, the fans sit at their minimum RPM even as the CPU climbs (one reporter: 70 °C, fans at ~1700–1800 RPM), and the daemon is completely silent about it — systemctl is-active t2fanrd still reports active, same PID as before suspend, no new log lines. This was reported from Omarchy 4.0.4-1 on a MacBookPro16,1.

Fix: The SMC clears the fan*_manual flag across suspend, and t2fanrd only writes that flag once at startup — so after resume the daemon keeps writing speeds the SMC ignores, and the firmware runs its own curve. Restart the service to re-assert manual control:

sudo systemctl restart t2fanrd

Verify it worked by checking the manual flag reads 1 again (under /sys/devices/.../APP0001:00/fan1_manual). As a standing workaround, the reporter runs a oneshot unit with WantedBy=suspend.target that restarts the service after resume — see omacom/omarchy#12393 for the same issue on a MacBookAir8,2. The proper upstream fix (re-writing the manual flag on every control-loop tick) was suggested but never landed before the repo was archived.

Daemon exits at boot — "CPU temperature sensor not found"

The service fails at boot with Error: CPU temperature sensor not found, and systemd gives up after hitting the start limit within about a second — leaving the fans on the firmware curve until someone restarts the service by hand (one reporter found their CPU at 88 °C with fans at ~2500 RPM).

Fix: The daemon looks for /sys/devices/platform/coretemp.0/hwmon/hwmon*/temp1_input exactly once, and at boot the service can start before udev has loaded the coretemp module. Restart it once the system is up:

sudo systemctl restart t2fanrd

The suggested upstream fix — retrying the sensor lookup for ~30 seconds before exiting — was never implemented before archiving. If this bites you on every boot, the durable workaround is a service override that delays the start until the sensor exists (e.g. systemctl edit t2fanrd and an ExecStartPre that waits for the temp1_input path) — unverified on Omarchy; confirm the override syntax on a real machine before publishing it as a fix.

"Error: Fan not found" on a MacBookPro15,1

The daemon crashes immediately on every start with Error: Fan not found. The kernel log shows macsmc-acpi initializing fine, but the fan-identification keys (F0ID/F1ID) fail with mmio/get_key_info failed, ret: 0x84.

Fix: There is no fix in t2fanrd. This is a firmware limitation of the 2018 15" MacBook Pro (MacBookPro15,1) — the same missing keys were reported against the macOS-native SMCKit back in 2018. The reporter suggested a fallback (default to a fixed fan count and use the speed read/write keys directly), but it was never implemented. If you own this model, t2fanrd will not work for you; the hwmon + fancontrol path the README points to is the thing to try instead — unverified, needs testing on that exact model.

GPU gets hot but the fans don't spin up

On a dual-GPU machine (reported on a Mac Pro 7,1 with a Radeon Pro 580X), the AMD GPU hits 100 °C under load while the fans sit near idle (~500 RPM) — because the CPU is barely working and t2fanrd only reads CPU temperature. Sustained, the machine freezes and restarts.

Fix: There is no config option to add a GPU sensor — t2fanrd reads the CPU and nothing else, and there is no per-fan minimum-speed setting either (that's open feature request #13). The reporter's workaround is to lower low_temp (e.g. into the low 40s) so the fans engage sooner — but that makes the fans cycle on and off noisily during light use. A steadier mitigation is always_full_speed=true on the affected fans during GPU-heavy sessions, then back to false after. Neither is a real fix; if you game or render on a dual-GPU T2 Mac, this limitation should decide whether t2fanrd is enough for you.

Pairs well with / If you hate this, try

Pairs well with

  • linux-t2 — the T2-patched kernel t2fanrd depends on; without it there is no fan driver for the daemon to talk to. apple-bcm-firmware-fetcher — pulls the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth firmware out of macOS so the rest of the machine works alongside the fans. apple-t2-audio-config — the audio counterpart, same "make the T2 Mac whole" job. And lm_sensors — sensors is how you actually see temperatures and fan RPM, since t2fanrd has no display of its own.

If you hate this, try

  • fancontrol (ships with lm_sensors) — the standard Linux fan daemon, which the archived README itself now recommends: write 1 to /sys/module/macsmc_hwmon/parameters/fan_control and let fancontrol drive the fans through the kernel's hwmon interface. More moving parts (you write your own fancontrol config via pwmconfig), but it's maintained and it can watch GPU sensors too. Or mbpfan — the older MacBook fan daemon, if you're on a pre-T2 Mac; it was built for the applesmc driver era, not T2 hardware.

Verdict: If you're on a T2 Mac and you just want the fans handled, t2fanrd is still the fastest path — one command, one config file, sensible defaults. Pick fancontrol if you have a dual-GPU machine (it can watch the GPU sensor t2fanrd ignores) or if you want a daemon with a future. Pick mbpfan only if your Mac predates the T2 chip. Macs Fan Control isn't an option on Linux at all — it's listed here because it's the first thing ex-macOS users search for.

t2fanrd is the free fix for the two bad defaults on a T2 Mac running Linux

There is no paid Linux fan daemon for T2 Macs to undercut — the honest pitch is different. t2fanrd is the free fix for the two bad defaults on a T2 Mac running Linux: fans screaming at full speed, or fans asleep while the machine cooks. The alternative most people actually live with is rebooting into macOS whenever the machine gets loud or hot, which defeats the point of running Omarchy on it. t2fanrd costs $0, one command, and a four-line config — what you give up is a GUI, GPU-aware curves, and an upstream maintainer (archived Nov 2026). What you keep is a quiet machine that doesn't throttle itself to death. If the GPU-blindness matters to you, the free upgrade path is fancontrol (above), not a purchase.

How to switch from macOS fan control to t2fanrd (~15 minutes)

  1. Install: On Omarchy: omarchy pkg add t2fanrd, then sudo systemctl enable --now t2fanrd.
  2. Check the baseline: Run sensors before and after starting the daemon. Note idle CPU temp and fan RPM with the daemon off (firmware curve) versus on.
  3. Tune the curve: Edit /etc/t2fand.conf — most people start by lowering low_temp from 55 to 45–50 if the fans engage too late, or raising it if they're too eager. Restart after each change: sudo systemctl restart t2fanrd.
  4. Test suspend: Suspend and resume once, then check sensors under load. If the fans are stuck at minimum, you have the issue #16 bug — set up the post-resume restart (see above) before you trust the machine unattended.
  5. What doesn't transfer: Your macOS fan presets and per-app rules (Macs Fan Control doesn't exist on Linux), and any temperature-based rules that watched the GPU — t2fanrd is CPU-only. Uninstall nothing on the macOS side; the two OSes don't share fan settings.

Frequently asked questions

Does t2fanrd work on Omarchy?

Yes — it's in the official Omarchy repo as t2fanrd (version r16.48baf96-2, built Nov 16, 2026) and installs with one command: omarchy pkg add t2fanrd. It only works on Intel Macs with the Apple T2 chip, and only with a T2-patched kernel (the linux-t2 package). It does nothing on a normal PC or an Apple Silicon Mac — there are no fans for it to find, and it will exit with "Fan not found."

Is t2fanrd really free?

Yes. GPL-3.0, no paid tier, no account. The Omarchy package is 263 KB to download and 530.4 KB installed, with only gcc-libs and glibc as dependencies.

Is it safe — what happens if the daemon crashes?

Unverified on a real machine, so treat this as "what the evidence suggests," not a tested fact. What is confirmed: the daemon takes manual control of the fans from the SMC, and when that manual flag is cleared (observed across suspend), the SMC firmware resumes running its own fan curve — the machine does not lose all cooling, it falls back to Apple's firmware behaviour. What is not confirmed is the exact fan state in the seconds after a crash — whether the fans stick at their last written speed or the SMC reclaims control immediately. Until someone tests a kill mid-run, don't run a heavy compile with the daemon stopped, and watch sensors the first time you use it.

Why is the project archived?

The maintainer archived it on Nov 16, 2026, because recent kernels expose T2 fans through the standard hwmon interface — the job no longer needs a T2-specific daemon. The README says standard userspace fan daemons "should work" after writing 1 to /sys/module/macsmc_hwmon/parameters/fan_control, and points users who want the t2fand config format at the sharpenedblade fork. The Omarchy package tracks that fork. Archival doesn't mean the package stops working — it means no new fixes, including for the suspend and boot-race bugs above.

How do I see my fan speed?

t2fanrd has no display. Install lm_sensors and run sensors — the applesmc-acpi-0 block shows each fan's RPM, min, and max, and coretemp-isa-0000 shows the CPU temperature the curve is reading.

My fans are stuck at minimum after waking the laptop. Is the daemon broken?

Probably not broken — this is the known suspend bug (issue #16). The SMC clears manual fan control across suspend and the daemon never re-asserts it, silently. sudo systemctl restart t2fanrd restores control. Set up a post-resume restart so you don't have to remember.

Can I set a minimum fan speed so the fans never sit at idle?

Not in t2fanrd — there is no minimum-speed option (open feature request #13). The workarounds are lowering low_temp so the curve engages earlier, or always_full_speed=true, which is far too blunt for daily use. If a minimum speed matters to you, fancontrol is the better tool.

Does it work on a MacBookPro15,1 (2018 15")?

Known not to: the daemon exits with "Fan not found" on that model because its firmware doesn't expose the fan-identification keys t2fanrd reads (issue #17). Try the hwmon + fancontrol path instead.
